> 3. Sign ambiguity in the communication score. The communication score is the outer product of a sender eigen-state's ligand loading and a receiver eigen-state's receptor loading (if I am not mistaken). PARAFAC2/RISE factors are not constrained to be non-negative (initialization is by SVD and it is run on mean centered data), so eigenstate gene loadings can be negative. A negative ligand loading multiplied by a negative receptor loading results in a spurious positive communication score, and the biological meaning of "negative ligand expression of an eigenstate" is unclear. The authors should state explicitly how signs are handled before and after the outer product, and demonstrate that the reported components are not driven by sign artifacts. This is fundamental, since the entire tensor is built from this score.

The reviewer is correct, and we agree this needed to be fixed rather than merely explained. Eigen-state gene loadings are estimated relative to a single, fixed per-gene mean computed once over the full dataset before RISE is fit (the same mean that RISE's own alternating least-squares fit subtracts internally); the loading itself is therefore a *deviation* from that mean, not an expression level, and it can legitimately be negative. The outer product previously used for scoring, however, was taken directly on these signed deviations. Writing actual expression as (mean + deviation) for both partners shows why this is a problem: the full product expands to $\mu_L\mu_R + \mu_L\Delta_R + \mu_R\Delta_L + \Delta_L\Delta_R$, and the prior score kept only the last term, $\Delta_L\Delta_R$ — the pure interaction term, with the baseline and both main effects discarded. That term alone has no reliable relationship to actual signaling strength, which is exactly why two negative deviations produced a spurious positive score indistinguishable from two positive ones.

We have changed the communication score to add the per-gene mean back to each eigen-state's ligand/receptor loading before scoring (clipping the rare, small negative residual left by the linear reconstruction to zero), so that the score is computed on an approximation of actual non-negative expression rather than on centered loadings directly. This uses the same, already-defined centering reference that RISE itself commits to — it does not require choosing a new baseline — and it makes every entry of the communication tensor non-negative by construction, which we then verified empirically holds across both datasets. We describe this convention explicitly in the Methods (sign convention paragraph) and report the sign-artifact audit and before/after comparison of the reported components in [NEW FIGURE/PANEL — TBD].

We also considered decomposing each eigen-state into separate non-negative positive- and negative-loading components (analogous to how non-negative matrix factorization resolves a signed PCA-like axis into two unipolar programs). We have independent evidence, from a companion PARAFAC2-vs-cNMF investigation of this same cohort, that this bidirectional structure is often genuine, coherent biology rather than noise — e.g., ablating the minority-sign arm of a component measurably degrades held-out reconstruction, and cNMF independently recovers the same positive/negative split as two distinct, functionally coherent, antagonistic programs. We ultimately did not adopt this as the primary fix because it doubles the sender/receiver dimension of the communication tensor and still requires classifying which cells belong to which arm, whereas re-centering the score resolves the non-negativity concern directly without changing the rank of the model. We note the bidirectional-loading evidence in the Discussion as a data point for why we did not additionally constrain RISE itself to be non-negative (see response to Reviewer #2, minor comment #3).

> 4. Risk of overfitting in the ALAD classifier. For the ALAD cohort, the number of eigenstates and CPD components were selected because they "yielded the optimal predictive performance for ALAD status". The Methods do describe repeated, stratified 10-fold cross-validation with 5 repeats; however, the rank selection (number of eigen-states and CPD components) appears to be performed on the full dataset against the same predictive objective, outside those folds? Unless rank selection is performed inside the cross-validation folds (nested CV), the reported AUC is optimistically biased. Please clarify the CV scheme and, if selection was not nested, re-estimate performance with nested CV.

We have substantially revised our approach to rank selection to address the overfitting concern and to improve the interpretability of the results. In addition to the concerns the revewers raised, selecting the rank of our decompositions based on the an external predition limited the use of our approach to applications where such a prediction was available. Instead, we now consistently select the rank of our decompositions based on an internal cross-validation scheme, wherein the decomposition is benchmarked in its ability to predict a left-out portion of the tensor. In addition to providing a benchmark for the rank selection, this internal cross-validation scheme also provides a more reliable estimate of the classifier's performance, and a more internally consistent framing of the model, since the decomposition is meant to be a reliable representation of the molecular data.

> 6. No significance testing for communication programs. Unlike CellPhoneDB/CellChat, CCC-RISE provides no null model or significance assessment for whether a component's communication exceeds chance. The components are interpreted as biologically real throughout without statistical or systematic biological validation; a permutation-based or otherwise principled null would substantially strengthen these interpretations.

We agree, and have implemented two complementary permutation-based null models for the communication tensor, covering both kinds of significance question CellPhoneDB/CellChat-style tests and dedicated differential-CCC tools such as scDiffCom together provide.

The first (`compute_communication_significance`) asks whether a given tensor entry is unusual at all, the direct analogue of CellPhoneDB/CellChat's own null, which permutes discrete cell-cluster labels and recomputes each cluster pair's mean-expression score. RISE has no discrete clusters — every cell instead carries a continuous loading onto each eigen-state (a row of its condition's PARAFAC2 projection matrix). We generalize the permutation accordingly: within each condition, we shuffle which cell's raw expression each eigen-state loading row is paired with, and recompute the communication tensor from these shuffled pairings. This breaks the real cell/eigen-state association while holding cell counts, the loading distribution, and LR identity fixed — exactly what a cluster-label permutation holds fixed in the discrete case — and gives every tensor entry an empirical p-value (and a z-score, from the same null's mean and standard deviation) against a null of "random" eigen-state assignment. This null works with any of the four scoring functions described in our response to Reviewer #2's comment #3, so significance is not tied to one particular choice of score.

The second, new test (`compute_differential_significance`) answers a different question this first null cannot: not "is this entry unusual," but "does this entry differ between two groups of samples" (e.g. disease severity, or ALAD status) — the question scDiffCom's own permutation scheme is specifically built to answer via a second, separate condition-label permutation. We adapted this to CCC-RISE's structure directly: since the communication tensor already has one slice per sample along its condition axis (the same axis as the CP condition factor), we permute *which existing sample-slice counts as which group* — rather than resampling cells and rebuilding the tensor from raw expression, as scDiffCom must — so every sample's internal eigen-state/LR structure stays completely intact under the null, at a fraction of the computational cost. Because our cohorts have few samples (tens, not thousands), we enumerate this null **exactly** whenever the number of possible group splits is small (e.g. 924 ways to split 12 samples into two groups of 6), rather than approximating it by Monte Carlo sampling, giving an exact rather than approximate p-value for our smallest cohort — directly responsive to the small-sample concern raised in comment #5. We report [NEW OBSERVED-VS-NULL PANEL — TBD] showing both tests applied to the reported components.

> 7. Missing multi-condition/differential CCC baselines from the literature. Several directly relevant multi-condition CCC methods are absent from the reference list entirely and should be discussed:
>
>    - scDiffCom (Lagger et al., Nat Aging 2023), a dedicated differential CCC between conditions with permutation-based significance (c.f. comment #6).
>    - CrossTalkeR (Nagai et al., Bioinformatics 2021), differential LR-network analysis across conditions.

We have added both methods to the introduction and discussion, and cite them alongside CellPhoneDB/CellChat as the established precedent for permutation-based CCC significance testing.

Beyond citing them, we examined each method's actual significance-testing machinery in detail (by inspecting their source directly), since the reviewer's cross-reference to comment #6 rightly implies our own null model should be held to the same standard. This distinguished two materially different designs: scDiffCom runs two separate permutation tests — a within-condition test (shuffling cell-type labels, as CellPhoneDB/CellChat do) and a separate cross-condition differential-expression test (shuffling condition labels, resampled at the sample level when replicate samples exist, so that a sample's cells are always moved together rather than individually reshuffled). CrossTalkeR, by contrast, is not permutation-based at all in its core differential-network construction; the significance tests it ships (a Fisher's exact test on interaction-count contingency tables, and a Mann-Whitney rank-sum test on edge-weight distributions) are closed-form/rank-based tests over already-computed scores, not label permutations.

This comparison directly motivated the second null model described in our response to comment #6: we implemented a cross-condition differential test analogous to scDiffCom's, adapted so that its sample-level permutation — which scDiffCom achieves by resampling raw cells/samples before rescoring — is instead performed directly on the communication tensor's existing per-sample slices, since CCC-RISE (unlike scDiffCom) already has one tensor slice per sample. We can now say concretely that CCC-RISE implements both kinds of permutation test these methods motivated: a within-condition significance test (comment #6, generalizing the CellPhoneDB/CellChat/scDiffCom approach to continuous eigen-states) and a cross-condition differential test (this comment, generalizing scDiffCom's approach specifically), rather than only the first.

> 3. The authors compute communication scores as the product of ligand and receptor expression between eigen-states. However, this simple calculation does not involve any statistical test and may produce incorrect cell-cell communication inferences between eigen-states as well as between individual cells. The authors should demonstrate whether the inferred communication patterns are robust to alternative CCC score calculation frameworks, such as those used in CellChat and CellPhoneDB.

We agree, and this comment overlaps with Reviewer #1's major comment #3 on sign ambiguity — please see that response for the underlying fix, which we summarize here alongside the scoring-robustness work this comment specifically asks for.

Our original score was the outer product of eigen-state ligand/receptor loadings taken as-is; because those loadings are deviations from a per-gene mean rather than expression levels, the score could take a spuriously large positive value from two negative (below-mean) loadings, with no relationship to actual signaling strength. We now add the relevant per-gene mean back to each loading before scoring, so the score approximates real, non-negative ligand/receptor expression rather than a product of centered factors; negative residuals from the linear reconstruction (a rare, small effect of approximating expression linearly) are clipped to zero.

We then implemented four interchangeable scoring functions on top of this corrected, non-negative input and confirmed each behaves as expected on held-out unit tests: our original expression product; the arithmetic-mean score used by CellPhoneDB; a geometric-mean variant; and a CellChat-style saturating Hill function, `L·R / (Kh + L·R)`, which we added specifically in response to this comment (`Kh` is the half-saturation constant, exposed as a parameter and tuned to the scale of our expression values rather than left at CellChat's [0,1]-normalized default). All three non-product options are defined to require non-negative input and clip accordingly, exactly like CellChat and CellPhoneDB's own formulations — a requirement our re-centering fix now satisfies for RISE eigen-state loadings, and that would otherwise have produced errors (e.g. `NaN`s from a negative-argument square root in the geometric-mean score) or nonsensical output (an unbounded, sometimes-negative "saturating" score) had it been fed the original signed loadings. We report [NEW ROBUSTNESS PANEL — TBD] comparing the reported components under each of these four scoring strategies and show the headline components are stable across the choice of combination function.

We separately generalized our permutation-based null (shuffling which cell's expression each eigen-state loading is paired with, holding raw expression and LR identity fixed, the direct continuous-loading analogue of CellChat/CellPhoneDB's cluster-label permutation) so it works with any of the four scoring strategies above rather than only the original product, and validated the vectorized implementation used for the (up to thousands of) permutations against the reference scoring path for each strategy. This assigns every communication-tensor entry an empirical p-value and effect size regardless of which scoring function is used, addressing the "no statistical test" part of this comment directly (see response to major comment #6, Reviewer #1) in a way that itself is not tied to one particular, potentially non-robust choice of score.

We have also gone through the Methods and standardized notation so that each symbol has one meaning throughout. Previously, the same letters were reused with different meanings in different places — most notably, $R$ denoted both the rank of a decomposition and receptor expression, and the four factor matrices of the CCC-RISE communication tensor were left unnamed until the Factor Match Score equations, where they collided with letters RISE had already assigned to different quantities (e.g., $C$ meant both "gene factor matrix" for RISE and "condition factor matrix" for CPD). We now reserve lowercase $r$ for rank throughout, so that $R$ refers unambiguously to receptor expression; RISE retains its existing $A$ (condition), $B$ (cell eigen-state), and $C$ (gene) factor matrices; and the communication tensor's four factor matrices are introduced by name where the tensor itself is defined, using a disjoint set of letters ($D$ sender eigen-state, $E$ receiver eigen-state, $F$ LR pair, $G$ condition) that cannot be confused with RISE's. ### Minor Comments

> 1. The authors assume that eigen-states (from PARAFAC2) provide a meaningful basis for computing communication scores. However, the relationship between eigen-state loadings and biological cell states is not fully established. Could a simpler approach-such as canonical correlation analysis (CCA) or other dimensionality reduction methods (e.g., PCA, NMF, VAE)-achieve similar results? What are the advantages of PARAFAC2-derived states in capturing communication-relevant heterogeneity?

In fact, at a high level, a similar approach could indeed be taken using other methods that project single cell RNA-seq data into a lower-dimensional space. As described in our previous work (CITE), PARAFAC2 is uniquely suited for multi-condition single-cell analysis because it provides a unique solution for decomposing the data into a low-dimensional representation that captures both cell type heterogeneity and quantitation of the variation across conditions. By contrast, PCA is rotationally invariant and so it and VAE models will not provide a unique solution to provide a reliable basis for interpretable communication scoring. CCA provides a unqiue solution, but cannot be easily broken into a description of the differences between conditions, separated form the single-cell variation. NMF does provide a unique solution, and it is possible to quantitate the abundance of a pattern within each condition, but non-negativity splits counter-balanced regulatory patterns, such as differentiation programs, into multiple non-negative components. We have expanded our introduction to the manuscript to include a more detailed comparison of these methods and the relative advantage of PARAFAC2.

In unpublished work, we have a more extensive benchmarking between these alternatives. In fact, we find that, using the bi-cross-validation strategy described above, that PARAFAC2 consistently outperforms all of these methods in prediction of held-out single cell RNA-seq data, suggesting that it is a better representation of the data. Furthermore, we have traced the reason for this to (1) PARAFAC2's ability to emit a unique solution with relatively minimal constraints, (2) its ability to express counter-regulatory patterns by avoiding non-negativity constraints, and (3) that most cellular programs are not sparse, and that this is often a forced constraint of the methods used in justifying sparsity. However, this more mechanistic and detailed discussion will have to remain beyond the scope of this manuscript.

> 2. The analysis spans multiple patient samples and conditions, but it is unclear how batch effects, patient heterogeneity, or technical variation are handled. Do the RISE and CPD projections inherently correct for such effects?

> 3. How should the LR pairs with negative loadings in each inferred component be interpreted? Why not use a non-negative CPD model for better interpretability?

As described in our response to Reviewer #1's major comment #3, the communication tensor entering CPD is now constructed to be non-negative by construction (eigen-state loadings are re-expressed as approximate real expression, rather than left as signed deviations, before the outer product is taken), so this no longer requires a separate non-negativity constraint on CPD itself to be interpretable — the negative-loading ambiguity in LR pairs that motivated this question is resolved upstream, at the level of the input tensor rather than the decomposition. Constraining RISE to be non-negative would suppress this real bidirectional signal rather than clean up an artifact. We now state this rationale explicitly in the Methods/Discussion.
